warmup.q: Researchers took a classic database program built to keep its data on disk, and loaded all of the data into memory, so it never had to wait for the disk. Then they counted the instructions the CPU ran for each order in a standard test. Where did most of the instructions go?
options: Waiting for the disk anyway, because the program still read its files
The real work: reading and changing the records each order needed
Bookkeeping built for disks: finding blocks of data in memory, locks, and a log for recovering from crashes
Copying data between the operating system and the program
warmup.why: Harizopoulos and colleagues measured Shore, a classic disk-based database, with all of its data in RAM. About a third of the instructions went to the code that manages pages in memory, and roughly 14%, 16% and 12% to latches, locks and the log. About 1/60 did the order's useful work. No disk reads happened, so the first option can't be it, and with everything in memory there was no copying from the operating system either. The second option is the tempting one, because work is what you'd expect a program to spend its time on. A store that lives in memory is fast mainly because it drops that bookkeeping. The first section starts there.

sections.h: Why a store that lives in memory is fast: no machinery built for disks
sections.html:
Let's start with a problem the payments program from Why caches work runs into. It runs as several copies on several servers, so that one crash doesn't stop the card readers. When a card reader gets no answer, it sends the same payment again, and the retry may reach a different copy. That copy must answer one question fast: have I already charged this payment? A HashMap inside each copy can't tell, because one copy can't see another's memory. The database can, for the price of a query on every check. What the copies need is one map they all share, kept in memory, on the network.

Would such a store beat a database that already holds all of its data in memory? It does, by a wide margin, and not for the reason most people guess. In 2008, Harizopoulos, Abadi, Madden and Stonebraker tested Shore, a classic database program built for disks. They loaded TPC-C, a standard test that imitates a company taking orders, into its memory, so no order ever waited for the disk. Then they counted the CPU's instructions. About a third went to the buffer manager, the code that finds pages (fixed-size blocks of data) in memory and holds them in place. The buffer pool, in the Storage engines track, built one. About 14% went to latches, short locks that stop two threads from changing one page at once. Another 16% went to locks on records, and 12% to writing the log that lets the program recover from a crash. Only about 1/60 of the instructions did the order's useful work, and stripping the rest made the program about 20 times faster.

So an in-memory store keeps its data as plain structures in memory, such as a hash table (the structure inside a HashMap) whose entries point straight at their values, and never turns them into pages and back. If it uses the disk at all, it writes a log or a snapshot on the side (Persistence and replication, lesson 9), and reads never come from that copy. Redis is the best-known store built this way.

The simplest shared map is a server holding a HashMap<String, byte[]> behind two commands, SET key value and GET key. It breaks as soon as the copies change values. Say two copies count a card's payments today. Both GET 41, both add one, and both SET 42, so one payment goes uncounted. (The worked example loses four counts in five this way.) So the server should know the shape of each value and change it itself. A key is a name such as payment:42, and its value has a type. Redis has strings, hashes (small maps of fields), lists, sets, sorted sets, and more in the next two lessons. INCR auths:card:7 adds one on the server. HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50 changes one field of a hash. A command that doesn't fit the value's type fails with WRONGTYPE. Types like these are easy to offer when everything lives in memory, and hard to build on pages of a disk.

Memory makes Redis fast, and the network decides how fast. On the lab machine, a GET from a Java program to Redis took about 214 microseconds from start to finish. Redis spent about half a microsecond of that running the command. That's the ladder from Why caches work again: the round trip is the expensive rung.

You'll meet Redis's twin, too. Redis was free software under the BSD license up to version 7.2. In March 2024, the company behind it moved 7.4 and later to licenses that let anyone read the code but limit how other companies may sell it as a service. Eight days later, the Linux Foundation launched Valkey, a fork (an independent copy) of Redis 7.2.4 under BSD, backed by AWS, Google Cloud and others. Redis 8.0 added AGPLv3, a free license, as a third choice. Today, Redis Open Source is at 8.10.3 (the labs pin redis:8.10.3) and Valkey at 9.1.3. Everything in this lesson works on both.

One server, and thousands of programs sending it commands at once. Next, we'll see how it serves them all.

try.title: Start Redis and poke it
steps: From the labs folder, start the server: docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this command starts Redis 8.10.3 in one, in the background.

Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli. redis-cli is Redis's own command-line tool: you type a command, and it prints the reply. Type the commands below, one at a time.
Before the last three, predict: what does TYPE say, and what happens when you GET a hash?
Leave the server running for the rest of the lesson. When you're done for the day, stop it and delete its data with docker compose -f env/redis.yml down -v.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
PING
SET payment:42 approved
GET payment:42
INCR auths:today
INCR auths:today
HSET payment:43 status approved amount 1250 currency EUR
HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50
TYPE payment:43

try.expect: PING answers PONG, and GET payment:42 prints "approved". The two INCRs print (integer) 1 and (integer) 2: the key didn't exist, so Redis started from 0. HSET prints (integer) 3 (three new fields), and HINCRBY prints (integer) 1300, worked out on the server. TYPE payment:43 says hash, and GET payment:43 fails with (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value. In the long INFO server output, find redis_version:8.10.3 and multiplexing_api:epoll. The second line says how Redis watches many connections at once: through epoll, a feature of Linux. The next section opens that up.

aside.title: So is Redis a cache or a database?
aside.html: It can be either, and the difference is in how you use it. When Redis holds copies of rows from a database, like the shop details in Why caches work, it's a cache: lose it, and the program fills it again. When it holds the only copy, like the note that a payment was already charged, it's the system of record, the place where the fact lives. Redis can write its data to disk so that a restart doesn't lose it, and lesson 9 shows how. Choose the settings for the job: a cache can afford to forget, and a record can't.

sections.h: One thread runs every command, one after another, to the end
sections.html:
Now the server has thousands of clients: programs connected to it over the network, all sending commands. A connection is an open line between two programs, and each client has its own. How should one server program serve them all?

The obvious design gives each connection its own thread, its own line of work. A program can run many threads at once, on different CPU cores or by taking turns. Each thread reads its client's command, runs it and writes the reply. This breaks in two places. Ten thousand connections need ten thousand threads, each with memory of its own, and the operating system spends much of its time switching between them. Worse, two threads can now touch the same key at the same moment. Two INCR auths:card:7 commands both read 41, both write 42, and one count is lost: the race from the last section, now inside the server. To stop it, every key needs a lock, a marker that lets only one thread in at a time. Then every command pays for locking, even when nobody else is near its key.

Redis goes the other way: one thread runs every command, like the clerk. But that thread must never sit waiting on one quiet connection while others have work. So it asks the operating system instead, through a system call, a request a program makes to the operating system. On Linux, that call is epoll_wait: "here are 10,000 connections; tell me which ones have bytes waiting, and let me sleep until at least one does." Then the thread serves only those. This loop is the event loop, and it repeats four steps:

  1. Ask the operating system which connections have bytes waiting. If none do, sleep until one does.
  2. For each ready client, read the bytes and cut them into complete commands.
  3. Run each command against memory, to the end, and put the reply in that client's outgoing buffer, a holding area for bytes not yet sent.
  4. Before sleeping again, send the waiting replies.

Step 3 is the picture to keep for the whole track. Commands from different clients never overlap. While INCR auths:card:7 runs, nothing else can read or write anything. So every single command is atomic: it happens as one step, and no client ever sees it half done. Fifty copies of the payments program calling INCR on one key never lose a count, and Redis needs no locks to promise that. Nobody else is running.

The price is the same fact seen from the other side. A command that takes 1.5 seconds holds the only thread for 1.5 seconds, and every other client waits, whatever key it wants. On the lab server, a GET costs about half a microsecond of that thread's time, so one 1.5-second command costs as much as three million GETs. The usual culprits are commands whose cost grows with the size of a key. KEYS * lists every key on the server. HGETALL and SMEMBERS read a whole key, which may hold a million entries. DEL of a huge key frees all of it at once. And a long Lua script holds the thread until it ends. A Lua script is a small program, in the Lua language, that Redis runs as one command. (Serial execution, in the Transactions track, puts scripts to work.) Here a script is the easiest way to keep Redis busy on purpose.

The post office picture holds, and it breaks only on speed. A clerk needs a minute per customer, and Redis about half a microsecond. So queues that would be hopeless at a post office stay invisible in Redis, until one slow request arrives. One thread runs every command to the end. A slow command makes everyone wait.

try.title: Freeze the server with one script
steps: Open two terminals (windows where you type commands) in the labs folder. In terminal 2, type this, but don't press Enter yet: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli GET payment:42.
In terminal 1, run the command below. Its Lua script spins on the server's CPU for 3,000 ms. Switch to terminal 2 at once and press Enter. Predict: when does "approved" appear?
Run the script again with 7000 in place of 3000, then the GET. Wait. When the GET gives up, stop the script from terminal 2: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SCRIPT KILL.

code.title: terminal 1
code.html: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli EVAL "local stop = os.clock() + ARGV[1] / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1" 0 3000

try.expect: The GET hangs, and prints "approved" a moment after terminal 1 prints (integer) 1. A different connection and an unrelated key made no difference. With 7000 ms the GET doesn't wait to the end. At the 5-second mark, it fails with (error) BUSY Redis is busy running a script. You can only call SCRIPT KILL or SHUTDOWN NOSAVE. Five seconds is the default busy-reply-threshold. From then on, Redis pauses the script now and then to answer other clients, but only with that error, so that you can send SCRIPT KILL. It prints OK, and terminal 1 gets (error) ERR Script killed by user with SCRIPT KILL.... The kill works only because the script hasn't written anything. A script that has written can only be stopped with SHUTDOWN NOSAVE, which stops the whole server.

video.title: One clerk for every window: how Redis runs each command

sections.h: Redis has several threads, and still only one runs commands
sections.html:
If one thread runs everything, two questions follow. Some jobs are slow by nature: writing a copy of 2 GB of data to disk, or freeing the memory of a key with ten million members. Who does those without freezing the loop? And the server has 8 or 16 CPU cores. Is one thread really all Redis uses?

For the slow chores, Redis hands the work to helpers that never run commands. The settings file that ships with Redis 8.10, redis.conf, calls Redis "mostly single threaded":

  • Background threads, named bio_* (background I/O, for input and output), close files and free memory. One of them also pushes Redis's log of writes, its record of every change, onto the disk with fsync, the system call that makes the disk really store the bytes. Delete a huge key with UNLINK, and it returns at once while a background thread frees the memory. Plain DEL frees it on the main thread, while everyone waits.
  • To save a snapshot of the whole dataset, Redis starts a copy of itself with fork, the system call that copies a running program. That child process writes the file, while the parent keeps serving clients (lesson 9).

For the cores, look at where the time goes for a small command. Running a GET takes half a microsecond. Reading the request from the connection, cutting it into a command and writing the reply are system calls plus copying, and together they often cost more than the command itself. So Redis 6 added I/O threads: helpers that do steps 2 and 4 of the loop, reading, cutting and writing, for many connections in parallel. The main thread still runs every command in step 3. Redis 8.0 shipped a new version of them.

I/O threads are off by default: the setting io-threads 1 means the main thread does all the reading and writing itself. The settings file says to turn them on only on machines with 4 or more cores, and to leave one core spare. That's 3 I/O threads on 4 cores, and 7 on 8. Redis measured up to 112% more throughput (requests handled per second) for 8.0, with 8 I/O threads on a server with many cores. That's the company's own test, and the gain depends on the mix of commands.

What I/O threads can't do is run two commands at once, or make one command faster. They help a server that spends its time moving bytes for many small commands over thousands of connections. They do nothing for one slow HGETALL. So when someone says "add threads", first ask which step of the loop is busy.

Other servers that work like Redis, such as Valkey, draw the line in other places, and Go deeper compares three of them. Whichever thread does the reading, the bytes follow one format. Next, we'll read it.

try.title: Count the server's threads
steps: List the threads of the running server with the command below. Inside its container, the server is process 1 (a process is a running program). Linux keeps one folder per thread under /proc/1/task, and the file comm in each holds the thread's name.

Start a throwaway server with four I/O threads: docker run --rm -d --name sfz-io4 -m 128m redis:8.10.3 redis-server --io-threads 4. List its threads with the same loop, using docker exec sfz-io4 in place of docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis.
Try to change it while it runs: docker exec sfz-io4 redis-cli CONFIG SET io-threads 2. Then remove it: docker rm -f sfz-io4.

code.title: terminal
code.html: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis sh -c 'for t in /proc/1/task/*; do cat $t/comm; done'

try.expect: The default server lists six threads: redis-server (the main thread, the only one that runs commands), bio_close_file, bio_aof, bio_lazy_free, and two jemalloc_bg_thd. Those last two belong to jemalloc, the code inside Redis that hands out memory. The --io-threads 4 server adds io_thd_1, io_thd_2 and io_thd_3; the main thread counts as I/O thread 0. CONFIG SET io-threads 2 fails with can't set immutable config: you pick the number of I/O threads when the server starts.

sections.h: Commands travel as RESP, and clients now speak RESP3
sections.html:
A connection carries a stream of bytes with no gaps or markers in it. If a client sends two commands quickly, the server may receive both in one read, or half of one. So both sides need a rule for where one command ends and the next begins.

The simplest rule is lines of text: SET payment:42 approved, then a newline. Redis still accepts that from a person typing into a raw connection. It breaks as soon as a value contains a space or a newline, and values do. A value might be a JSON document (a common text format for structured data), a saved Java object, or any bytes at all. Quoting rules would force the server to inspect every byte of every value.

The fix is to send each length first. That's RESP, the Redis serialization protocol: the agreed format for turning commands and replies into bytes. A command is an array of strings, each with its length in bytes in front:

*2\r\n$3\r\nGET\r\n$10\r\npayment:42\r\n

Read it as: an array (*) of 2 elements, a 3-byte string ($3) GET, and a 10-byte string payment:42. \r\n is a carriage return and a line feed, the two characters that end a line. Because the server knows each length in advance, it reads exactly that many bytes and never looks inside them. The first byte of a reply says what kind of reply it is: +OK is a short status, :42 a whole number, $8 an 8-byte string, $-1 no value, and -ERR an error.

That version is RESP2, the standard since Redis 2.0. It has one gap: structured replies come back as flat lists. HGETALL returns status, approved, amount, 1250, and the client has to know to pair them up. RESP3, available since Redis 6.0, adds real maps (%), sets (~), decimal numbers, true and false, a null (_), and push messages, which the server sends without being asked. Client-side caching, where Redis tells a program that its own copy is out of date, relies on those. Every connection starts in RESP2 and switches when the client sends HELLO 3.

Both client libraries in this track, Jedis and Lettuce, send HELLO 3 when they connect. Jedis 8 made that its default, and falls back to RESP2 if the server refuses. You'll rarely look at RESP yourself. You need it when a program between your code and Redis breaks the traffic, when a reply's type surprises your code, or when you read a recording of network traffic.

Nobody should write RESP by hand, though. Next, we'll pick a library that writes it for us.

try.title: Talk RESP over a plain connection
steps: Run RespDemo (Java) or RespDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. It opens a plain network connection (a socket) to port 6379, the number Redis listens on, with no library at all. It sends commands as raw RESP and prints every byte both ways, with \r\n made visible.
Before you look, predict the reply bytes for INCR auths:today and for INCR payment:42.
Compare HGETALL payment:45 and GET payment:404 before and after HELLO 3. What changed?

code.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.net.Socket; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; /** Speaks RESP to Redis over a plain socket, with no client library, and prints every byte. */ public class RespDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { try (Socket socket = new Socket("localhost", 6379)) { OutputStream out = socket.getOutputStream(); InputStream in = socket.getInputStream(); send(out, in, "PING"); send(out, in, "SET", "payment:42", "approved"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:42"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:404"); send(out, in, "INCR", "auths:today"); send(out, in, "INCR", "payment:42"); send(out, in, "HSET", "payment:45", "status", "approved", "amount", "1250"); send(out, in, "HGETALL", "payment:45"); send(out, in, "HELLO", "3"); // switch this connection to RESP3 send(out, in, "HGETALL", "payment:45"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:404"); } } // a command is an array of bulk strings: *<count>, then $<length> and the bytes of each word static void send(OutputStream out, InputStream in, String... words) throws IOException { StringBuilder cmd = new StringBuilder("*" + words.length + "\r\n"); for (String w : words) { cmd.append('$').append(w.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length).append("\r\n").append(w).append("\r\n"); } out.write(cmd.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); out.flush(); // good enough for a demo: on loopback a short reply arrives in one read byte[] buf = new byte[8192]; int n = in.read(buf); System.out.println("> " + show(cmd.toString(), 200)); System.out.println("< " + show(new String(buf, 0, n, StandardCharsets.UTF_8), 90)); } static String show(String s, int max) { String visible = s.replace("\r\n", "\\r\\n"); return visible.length() <= max ? visible : visible.substring(0, max) + "... (" + s.length() + " bytes)"; } }

(${s.length} bytes)" }

try.expect: PING gets +PONG , and the first INCR auths:today gets :1 (higher if you ran the first Try it). INCR payment:42 gets -ERR value is not an integer or out of range . Before HELLO 3, HGETALL payment:45 returns a flat array, *4 $6 status ..., and the client has to pair the items up itself. After it, the same command returns a map, %2 ..., holding two field-value pairs. A missing key is $-1 in RESP2 and _ in RESP3. The reply to HELLO 3 is itself a map of about 690 bytes (the exact size depends on your connection's id number) that starts with the server's name, version 8.10.3 and proto 3.

sections.h: This track uses Jedis, and Lettuce where Kotlin needs it
sections.html:
Nobody wants to count bytes by hand, so programs talk to Redis through a client library: code you add to your program that writes and reads RESP for you. Java has two popular ones, Jedis and Lettuce, and the choice that matters inside them is how your program's threads share connections.

The first design is a pool. The library keeps several connections open. A call borrows one, sends one command, waits for the reply and gives the connection back. While one thread waits, others use other connections. Every call blocks its thread: the thread stops and waits for one round trip. Threads queue when all the connections are busy. Jedis's pool holds at most 8 connections unless you configure more, so 200 threads on 8 connections take turns. This is Jedis.

The second design is multiplexing: one connection shared by every thread. Calls write their commands onto the same connection back to back, without waiting for each other. Redis answers the commands on a connection in the order they arrived, so the library keeps a queue of callers and hands each reply to the next caller in line. One connection carries thousands of calls at once. The cost is that your code gets something to wait on instead of a plain value. It might be a future (an object that will hold the answer later), a callback, or a paused coroutine, Kotlin's light way to wait without blocking a thread. This is Lettuce.

Jedis 8.0.2 gives you one RedisClient, built with RedisClient.builder(), with the pool behind it. Lettuce 7.9.0 offers four styles of call: plain blocking calls, futures (RedisFuture), a style built on a library called Project Reactor, which treats answers as streams of events, and Kotlin coroutines. The coroutine style needs two extra libraries and one annotation in your code, and the compare below shows them.

This track teaches with Jedis. One call is one command and one reply, so your code matches what you'd type at the redis-cli prompt, line for line. The lessons stay about Redis instead of about futures. Lettuce shows up where it changes the picture: Kotlin coroutines, and many calls sharing one connection.

One trap: both libraries name their main class RedisClient. In a file that uses both, write one of them with its full package name, as the Try it below does. Here's Jedis, in Java and then in Kotlin:

Java
RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build();
redis.set("payment:42", "approved");
String status = redis.get("payment:42");          // blocks until the reply arrives
Kotlin
val redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()
redis.set("payment:42", "approved")
val status: String? = redis.get("payment:42")     // GET of a missing key returns null

Now a program can talk to Redis. Next, we'll ask which types to store, and what each one costs in memory.

Read the last two lines. They're the server's own view of each connection, from the command CLIENT LIST.

code.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo; import io.lettuce.core.RedisFuture; import io.lettuce.core.api.StatefulRedisConnection; import io.lettuce.core.api.async.RedisAsyncCommands; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** The same GET through Jedis (blocking) and Lettuce (async), then how each one connected. */ public class ClientsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Jedis 8: one RedisClient, a pool of connections behind it, blocking calls try (RedisClient jedis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { jedis.set("payment:42", "approved"); System.out.println("Jedis GET payment:42 -> " + jedis.get("payment:42")); // Lettuce 7: one connection shared by every caller, calls return futures io.lettuce.core.RedisClient lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379"); try (StatefulRedisConnection<String, String> conn = lettuce.connect()) { RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> async = conn.async(); RedisFuture<String> reply = async.get("payment:42"); // returns at once System.out.println("Lettuce GET payment:42 -> " + reply.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // ask the server how each library connected String list = async.clientList().get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Pattern fields = Pattern.compile("(resp=\\d+) (lib-name=\\S+) (lib-ver=\\S+)"); for (String line : list.split("\n")) { Matcher m = fields.matcher(line); if (m.find() && !m.group(2).equals("lib-name=")) { System.out.println(m.group(1) + " " + m.group(2) + " " + m.group(3)); } } } finally { lettuce.shutdown(); } } } }

alt.title: ClientsDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo import io.lettuce.core.ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi import io.lettuce.core.api.coroutines import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient /** The same GET through Jedis (blocking) and Lettuce (coroutines), then how each one connected. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { // Jedis 8: one RedisClient, a pool of connections behind it, blocking calls RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { jedis -> jedis.set("payment:42", "approved") println("Jedis GET payment:42 -> " + jedis.get("payment:42")) // Lettuce 7: one connection shared by every caller; coroutines suspend instead of blocking val lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379") try { lettuce.connect().use { conn -> val redis = conn.coroutines() val list = runBlocking { println("Lettuce GET payment:42 -> " + redis.get("payment:42")) // suspends redis.clientList().orEmpty() // ask the server how each library connected } val fields = Regex("""(resp=\d+) (lib-name=\S+) (lib-ver=\S+)""") list.lineSequence() .mapNotNull { fields.find(it) } .filter { it.groupValues[2] != "lib-name=" } .forEach { println(it.groupValues.drop(1).joinToString(" ")) } } } finally { lettuce.shutdown() } } }

try.expect: Both versions print approved twice, then resp=3 lib-name=jedis lib-ver=8.0.2 and resp=3 lib-name=Lettuce lib-ver=7.9.0.RELEASE/1d7b2b2. Both libraries switched to RESP3 with HELLO 3, and both told the server their name and version with CLIENT SETINFO. So on a Redis that many programs share, CLIENT LIST shows which library and version every connection uses.

refs.title: Jedis v7 to v8 migration guide

opening:
Picture a small post office with one clerk and six windows. The clerk serves the first window, then the second, and so on round the room, finishing each job before starting the next. Most jobs take seconds, so the queues stay short. Then a customer asks for four hundred parcels to be weighed, and every window waits.

Redis, a program that keeps data in memory and answers requests over the network, works much like that clerk. A single thread, one line of work inside the program, runs every command, one at a time. It's easy to hear "one thread" and think "slow", and to reach for more threads when it stalls. Both instincts miss what's going on.

Why caches work showed that a copy kept close by answers most lookups, and that the copy often lives in Redis. In this lesson, we'll see why a store in memory is fast, follow its one thread through many clients, freeze it with one slow command, and connect from Java and Kotlin. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a post office clerk who serves every window in turn. Redis works the same way: one thread finishes each command before it starts the next. That makes every command atomic, and it lets one slow command hold up everyone.

With the lab server running, type SLOWLOG GET at the redis-cli prompt. It lists the commands that took longer than 10 ms, and how long each one took. Run this lesson's slow script first, and watch it turn up there.

Next, we'll look at the types Redis stores, and find out why one more item can make a key ten times bigger.

compare.title: Lettuce from Java and from Kotlin: one connection, two styles

java.title: PaymentStatus.java
java.html: // Lettuce async: every call returns a RedisFuture at once RedisClient client = RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379"); try (StatefulRedisConnection<String, String> conn = client.connect()) { RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> redis = conn.async(); RedisFuture<String> status = redis.get("payment:42"); RedisFuture<Long> auths = redis.incr("auths:today"); // both commands are already on the wire; now wait for the replies System.out.println(status.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) + " " + auths.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } finally { client.shutdown(); }

kotlin.title: PaymentStatus.kt
kotlin.html: // Lettuce coroutines: calls suspend instead of returning futures @OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun printStatus(client: RedisClient) { client.connect().use { conn -> val redis = conn.coroutines() coroutineScope { val status = async { redis.get("payment:42") } val auths = async { redis.incr("auths:today") } println("${status.await()} ${auths.await()}") } } }

compare.note: Both versions put two commands on one connection before waiting for either reply, so the INCR doesn't wait a whole round trip for the GET. Java does it with futures, objects that hold an answer once it arrives. Kotlin does it with coroutines, async and await, and the code reads from top to bottom. The coroutine style is a layer over Lettuce's reactive style, which is built on Project Reactor. That's why it needs the libraries kotlinx-coroutines-core and kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, and the annotation @ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi, which says you accept an API that may still change. Jedis code looks the same in both languages: it blocks, so there's nothing to translate.

worked.title: Count payments from eight threads without losing any

steps.say: A nightly job counts today's payments in Redis. Eight worker threads share one Jedis RedisClient, and each one reads the counter, adds 1 and writes it back. Predict what it prints after 8,000 calls.
steps.code: RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8); for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) { pool.submit(() -> { String v = redis.get("auths:today"); // 1. read long n = v == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong(v); // 2. add redis.set("auths:today", String.valueOf(n + 1)); // 3. write }); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES); System.out.println(redis.get("auths:today"));

alt.html: val redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build() val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) repeat(8_000) { pool.submit { val v: String? = redis.get("auths:today") // 1. read val n = v?.toLong() ?: 0L // 2. add redis.set("auths:today", (n + 1).toString()) // 3. write } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES) println(redis.get("auths:today"))

steps.say: Three runs against the lab server printed 1,611, then 1,654, then 1,628. About four counts in five vanished. Each command was atomic, but the pair wasn't. Between one thread's GET and its SET, the event loop ran other threads' commands, so several threads read the same old value and wrote the same new one. It's the race from the first section, with a network round trip widening the gap.
Let the server do the read, the add and the write as one command. INCR runs to the end inside the loop, so nothing can come between its read and its write. The same job now prints 8000 on every run.
steps.code: for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) { pool.submit(() -> redis.incr("auths:today")); // one command: read, add and write on the server }

alt.html: repeat(8_000) { pool.submit { redis.incr("auths:today") } // one command: read, add and write on the server }

steps.say: With Lettuce, all 8,000 INCRs can share a single connection, with no pool of threads at all. In Java, each incr returns a future at once, and CompletableFuture.allOf waits for all of them. In Kotlin, 8,000 coroutines each pause until their reply arrives, while the commands queue up on the one connection. The Kotlin version took about 230 ms on the lab server (it depends on your machine and Docker) and printed 8000.
steps.code: RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> redis = conn.async(); List<CompletableFuture<Long>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) calls.add(redis.incr("auths:today").toCompletableFuture()); CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])).join(); System.out.println(redis.get("auths:today").get()); // 8000

alt.html: val redis = conn.coroutines() coroutineScope { repeat(8_000) { launch { redis.incr("auths:today") } } // 8,000 coroutines, one connection } println(redis.get("auths:today")) // 8000

If nothing has arrived, set clock = pending.minOf { it.arrivedAt } and go round again. Without that, an idle loop spins forever and the test runs out of time.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> scripts.eval(BUSY_SCRIPT, 0, String.valueOf(scriptMillis))) runs the script in the background. Call join() on it before you return, so a script error fails the call.

drill.title: Write the slow-script probe from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write timeGetDuringScript(scripts, app, key, millis). It starts a busy Lua script on one client in the background, waits 200 ms, times a GET on the other client, waits for the script, and returns the GET's milliseconds. Write the Lua too. Then compare with the answer. Did you remember why the script needs its own thread?

answer.html: static final String BUSY = "local stop = os.clock() + tonumber(ARGV[1]) / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1"; static long timeGetDuringScript(RedisClient scripts, RedisClient app, String key, long millis) throws InterruptedException { CompletableFuture<Object> script = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync( () -> scripts.eval(BUSY, 0, String.valueOf(millis))); // eval blocks a pool thread, not us Thread.sleep(200); // head start: the script is running long t0 = System.nanoTime(); app.get(key); // waits for the script to end long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; script.join(); return ms; }

alt.html: const val BUSY = "local stop = os.clock() + tonumber(ARGV[1]) / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1" fun timeGetDuringScript(scripts: RedisClient, app: RedisClient, key: String, millis: Long): Long { val script = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { scripts.eval(BUSY, 0, millis.toString()) } // eval blocks a pool thread Thread.sleep(200) // head start: the script is running val t0 = System.nanoTime() app.get(key) // waits for the script to end val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 script.join() return ms }

recap: A store that lives in memory is fast mainly because it keeps data in plain structures. It skips the page handling, latches, locks and log records that a disk-based database runs even when all of its data is in memory.
Redis keeps typed values (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets) in memory, and commands such as INCR change them on the server, so a client rarely has to read, change and write back.
One thread runs every command, one after another, each to the end. That makes every single command atomic, without any locks.

The same fact is the limit: one slow command (KEYS *, HGETALL on a huge hash, a long Lua script) makes every other client wait. Background threads, a forked child and optional I/O threads (io-threads, off by default) do side work and never run commands, so more threads can't fix it.

Clients speak RESP, which sends the length of every piece before its bytes. Jedis 8 and Lettuce 7.9 switch to RESP3 with HELLO 3. This track teaches with Jedis's blocking RedisClient, and uses Lettuce for Kotlin coroutines and shared connections.
Redis 8 comes under RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3, and is at 8.10.3 now. Valkey (9.1.3) is the BSD-licensed fork, and both run everything in this lesson.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Redis has only one thread, so it can't keep up with us. Let's turn on I/O threads so it runs our commands in parallel." Explain what's right and what's wrong in that, in your own words.
explain.answer: Redis does run commands on one thread, one at a time, each to the end. That's why each command is atomic, and why one slow command makes everyone wait. But one thread is rarely the limit for small commands: a GET costs about half a microsecond. I/O threads don't run commands in parallel. They take over reading from connections, cutting the bytes into commands and writing replies, which helps when the server spends its time moving bytes for many connections. If our problem is that every request gets slow now and then, the likely cause is one slow command whose cost grows with the size of a key, and I/O threads won't touch it. I'd check SLOWLOG GET first, and replace the slow command with one that works in small steps, such as SCAN in place of KEYS.

deeper.html:
The 2008 measurement is worth reading in full. With its data in memory and logging on, Shore ran about 640 New Order transactions (one kind of order in the test) a second. The authors then removed one piece at a time: logging, locking, latching, then the buffer manager. The fully stripped engine ran about 12,700 a second on one thread, about 20 times faster, and a hand-written program doing only the useful work about 46,500. No single piece dominated, which is why tuning one of them in a disk-based database never closes the gap. H-Store, a research system, and VoltDB after it came from the same group and the same argument. Split the data into parts, run each part's work one job at a time on one thread, and keep everything in memory. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 4, makes the same point about in-memory databases and cites this paper.

Why is one thread fast enough? Most commands touch one key and finish in well under a microsecond, and the data is already in RAM. With no second thread, there are no locks to take, and no data passed back and forth between the caches of different CPU cores. For small commands, the expensive part is usually the system calls: one read and one write per command per client. Pipelining attacks that cost: send many commands, read many replies, and pay for the system calls once (Serial execution, in the Transactions track, uses it). I/O threads spread the same cost over several cores.

The real loop is a little richer than the lab's model. When a client has sent several commands at once, Redis reads a buffer's worth of bytes and runs every complete command in it before moving on to the next client. That's why a pipelined batch from one client runs back to back, and why a client that sends a huge batch can delay the clients after it in the same pass.

A tip for writing busy scripts. On the lab server, a script that looped on redis.call('TIME') until 2,000 ms had passed ran for 5 seconds instead. Inside a script, TIME kept returning the moment the script started, and it moved only when the 5-second busy handling began. os.clock() measures the CPU time the script has used, which keeps moving, so the lab uses it. A script that waits on the server's clock won't work for the same reason, and you shouldn't want a script that waits anyway.

Other servers that speak Redis's protocol split the work differently. Valkey 8.0 reworked its I/O threads to run alongside the main thread and hand it commands in batches. Its announcement reports up to 1.2 million requests a second on one AWS machine, up from 380,000 (again the makers' own figure). It still runs commands on one thread. Dragonfly splits the keys into shards, one per thread, so every core runs commands for its own keys. That buys throughput, and the price is coordination whenever one command touches keys in two shards. In version 2.1 (November 2026), Dragonfly moved to its own source-available license, free in production up to 100 vCPUs. Memcached, the older pure cache, runs several worker threads over one shared table guarded by locks, and stores only plain bytes.

The licenses in detail: Redis 7.4 to 7.8 came under RSALv2 or SSPLv1, Redis's own license and MongoDB's, both of which let you read and change the code but restrict offering it as a service. From 8.0, you may also take it under AGPLv3, a free license that asks anyone who offers a changed version over a network to publish their changes. Jedis and Lettuce themselves are under the MIT license.

Lettuce is built on Netty, a Java library for network programs. Netty runs an event loop of its own, so a Lettuce connection and the Redis server it talks to work in much the same way.

If you want the source, src/ae.c in the Redis repository is the event loop library (it wraps epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS), and src/networking.c reads commands and writes replies.
